questions.question: A circle has a radius of 5. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area of a circle = πr². With r = 5: Area = π(5²) = 25π.
questions.trap: Using diameter (10) instead of radius (5) in the formula gives π(10²) = 100π.

questions.ets_note: Single-formula plug-in; too trivial and the figure adds nothing.

questions.question: What is the circumference of a circle with diameter 14?
questions.explanation: Circumference = 2πr = πd. With diameter = 14: C = π(14) = 14π.
questions.trap: Using r = 14 instead of r = 7 gives C = 2π(14) = 28π. Always check if the given value is radius or diameter.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 210 215" width="210" height="215" role="img"><circle cx="105.0" cy="105.0" r="72.0" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><circle cx="105" cy="105" r="2.4" fill="#16191d"/><line x1="33.0" y1="105.0" x2="177.0" y2="105.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="105.0" y="97.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle" style="">14</text></svg>
questions.ets_note: Plain formula recall.

questions.question: A circle has circumference 10π. What is its radius?
questions.explanation: Circumference = 2πr. Set 2πr = 10π. Divide both sides by 2π: r = 10π / 2π = 5.
questions.trap: Forgetting to divide by 2 and concluding r = 10 because C = 10π.

questions.question: A circle has a radius of 6. What is the length of an arc subtended by a central angle of 60°?
questions.trap: Using diameter (12) instead of radius (6): (1/6) × 2π(12) = 4π. The arc length formula uses radius.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 230 235" width="230" height="235" role="img"><circle cx="115.0" cy="115.0" r="80.0" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><path d="M 115 115 L 115.0 35.0 A 80 80 0 0 1 184.3 75.0 Z" fill="#d8e1e9" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="130.0" y="93.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle" style="">60°</text><text x="127.0" y="75.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start" style="">6</text></svg>
questions.ets_note: Easy formula recall; figure fine.

questions.question: What is the area of a sector with radius 4 and central angle 90°?
questions.trap: Computing arc length instead of sector area: (90/360) × 2π(4) = 2π. The sector area formula uses πr², not 2πr.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 230 235" width="230" height="235" role="img"><circle cx="115.0" cy="115.0" r="80.0" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><path d="M 115 115 L 115.0 35.0 A 80 80 0 0 1 195.0 115.0 Z" fill="#d8e1e9" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="136.2" y="97.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle" style="">90°</text><text x="127.0" y="75.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start" style="">4</text></svg>

questions.question:
Circle A has radius 3. Circle B has radius 6.

Quantity A: Area of Circle A
Quantity B: One-fourth the area of Circle B
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Circle A area = π(3²) = 9π. Circle B area = π(6²) = 36π, and one-fourth of that = 9π. Quantity A = 9π = Quantity B, so the quantities are equal.
questions.trap: Assuming that because radius doubles, one-fourth the area equals the smaller circle. Actually this is exactly true: if r₂ = 2r₁, then πr₂²/4 = π(2r₁)²/4 = 4πr₁²/4 = πr₁². The two are equal.

questions.question: A circle has area 36π. What is its diameter?
questions.explanation: Area = πr² = 36π, so r² = 36, r = 6. Diameter = 2r = 2(6) = 12.
questions.trap: Stopping at r = 6 and reporting the radius instead of the diameter.

questions.question: A semicircle has a diameter of 8. What is the area of the semicircle? (Give your answer in terms of π — enter the coefficient of π only.)
questions.explanation: Full circle area = πr² where r = 4 (half of diameter 8). Full area = 16π. Semicircle area = 16π/2 = 8π. The coefficient is 8.
questions.trap: Using diameter 8 as radius: π(8²)/2 = 32π. Always halve the diameter to get radius.
questions.ets_note: "Enter coefficient of pi only" is un-ETS; ETS would use MCQ with pi options.

questions.question: A circle has radius r. If the radius is tripled, the new area is how many times the original area?
questions.explanation: Original area = πr². New radius = 3r. New area = π(3r)² = 9πr². Ratio = 9πr²/πr² = 9.
questions.trap: Thinking area scales linearly with radius and answering 3. Area scales with the square of radius.

questions.question: What is the central angle of a sector whose arc length is one-third of the circle's circumference?
questions.explanation: Arc length = (θ/360) × circumference. If arc = (1/3) × circumference, then θ/360 = 1/3, so θ = 360/3 = 120°.
questions.trap: Confusing the fraction of the circumference with the angle fraction and computing 360 × (1/3) incorrectly or arriving at 90°.
questions.ets_note: Trivial one-step; vague trap text.

questions.question: A circle has radius 10. A chord is drawn such that it is 6 units from the center. What is the length of the chord?
questions.explanation: Draw a radius to one end of the chord and a perpendicular from the center to the chord. This creates a right triangle with hypotenuse = radius = 10 and one leg = 6 (perpendicular distance). The other leg (half the chord length) = √(10² - 6²) = √(100 - 36) = √64 = 8. Full chord length = 2 × 8 = 16.
questions.trap: Forgetting to double the half-chord: reporting 8 instead of 16.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 210 215" width="210" height="215" role="img"><circle cx="105.0" cy="105.0" r="72.0" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><circle cx="105" cy="105" r="2.4" fill="#16191d"/><line x1="105.0" y1="105.0" x2="177.0" y2="105.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="141.0" y="97.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle" style="">10</text></svg>
questions.ets_note: Figure shows only a radius, not the chord or the 6; distractor 18 is filler.

questions.question: The area of a sector is 12π and the radius of the circle is 6. What is the central angle of the sector?
questions.explanation: Sector area = (θ/360) × πr². So 12π = (θ/360) × π(36) = (θ/360) × 36π. Dividing both sides by 36π: 12/36 = θ/360 → 1/3 = θ/360 → θ = 120°.
questions.trap: Setting up 12π = (θ/360) × 6π (using radius instead of r²) and getting θ = 720°, which is impossible.

questions.question: Two concentric circles have radii 5 and 9. What is the area of the ring (annulus) between them? (Enter the coefficient of π only.)
questions.explanation: Area of ring = Area of large circle − Area of small circle = π(9²) − π(5²) = 81π − 25π = 56π. Coefficient = 56.
questions.trap: Subtracting radii first: π(9−5)² = π(4²) = 16π. You must subtract the areas, not compute π(r₂−r₁)².
questions.ets_note: Stem says 'enter the coefficient of π only'; 'annulus' parenthetical textbookish.

questions.question: An inscribed angle in a circle measures 35°. What is the measure of the central angle that subtends the same arc?
questions.explanation: The inscribed angle theorem states that a central angle is twice the inscribed angle that subtends the same arc. Central angle = 2 × 35° = 70°.
questions.trap: Confusing the relationship: dividing instead of multiplying, getting 35/2 = 17.5°.
questions.ets_note: Direct theorem recall, one step; labelled medium but is easy.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Single application of the inscribed angle theorem (double it).

questions.question:
A circle has radius 7.

Quantity A: Arc length of a 60° sector
Quantity B: One-sixth of the circumference
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Quantity A: Arc length = (60/360) × 2π(7) = (1/6) × 14π = 7π/3. Quantity B: (1/6) × 2π(7) = (1/6) × 14π = 7π/3. They are identical — a 60° arc IS one-sixth of the circumference since 60/360 = 1/6.
questions.trap: Thinking the arc length formula gives a different result from the direct fraction. They are the same calculation.
questions.ets_note: Both quantities same by definition; trivial.

questions.question: A square is inscribed in a circle of radius 5. What is the area of the square?
questions.explanation: When a square is inscribed in a circle, the diagonal of the square equals the diameter of the circle. Diameter = 2(5) = 10. If side of square = s, then diagonal = s√2 = 10, so s = 10/√2 = 5√2. Area = s² = (5√2)² = 50.
questions.trap: Setting the side equal to the radius (5) and computing area = 25. The diagonal, not the side, equals the diameter.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 240 250" width="240" height="250" role="img"><circle cx="120.0" cy="120.0" r="85.0" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><polygon points="180.1,180.1 59.9,180.1 59.9,59.9 180.1,59.9" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="120.0" y1="120.0" x2="180.1" y2="59.9" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-dasharray="5,4"/><text x="164.0" y="86.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start" style="">5</text></svg>
questions.ets_note: Options 25,50,25sqrt2,25pi,100 not ascending (25sqrt2≈35).

questions.question: A circle has radius 10. Which of the following could be the arc length of a sector of this circle, if a sector may be the entire circle? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The circumference is 2π(10) = 20π. The arc of a sector (the full circle allowed) can have any length greater than 0 and at most 20π. A: 5π ≤ 20π, true (a 90° sector). B: 10π ≤ 20π, true (a semicircle). C: 20π equals the circumference, true (the full circle). D: 40π is twice the circumference, false. E: 100π is the circle's area πr², not an arc length, false.
questions.trap: Treating the area πr² = 100π as an arc length (E), or doubling the circumference to 4πr = 40π (D). Some students also reject 20π because a full circle does not look like a sector.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 210 215" width="210" height="215" role="img"><circle cx="105.0" cy="105.0" r="72.0" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><circle cx="105" cy="105" r="2.4" fill="#16191d"/><line x1="105.0" y1="105.0" x2="177.0" y2="105.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="141.0" y="97.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle" style="">10</text></svg>
questions.ets_note: Key makes all five options correct (degenerate); E hinges on whether a full circle is a sector.

changes: stated that a sector may be the entire circle so 20π is admitted

questions.question: A circle has radius 12. What is the length of an arc that subtends a central angle of 150°?
questions.trap: Using 150/360 = 5/12 correctly but then multiplying by πr (= 12π) instead of 2πr (= 24π): (5/12) × 12π = 5π.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 230 235" width="230" height="235" role="img"><circle cx="115.0" cy="115.0" r="80.0" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><path d="M 115 115 L 115.0 35.0 A 80 80 0 0 1 155.0 184.3 Z" fill="#d8e1e9" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="144.0" y="111.2" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle" style="">150°</text><text x="127.0" y="75.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start" style="">12</text></svg>

questions.question:
Circle P has radius r. Circle Q has circumference equal to the area of Circle P.

Quantity A: Radius of Circle Q
Quantity B: r²/2
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Area of Circle P = πr². Circumference of Circle Q = πr². So 2πR = πr² where R is radius of Q. Solving: R = πr²/(2π) = r²/2. Quantity A = r²/2 = Quantity B. They are equal.
questions.trap: Setting area of P equal to area of Q (instead of circumference of Q) giving R = r, then concluding Quantity B = r²/2 < r for r > 2.

questions.question: A circle is centered at the origin and passes through the point (3, 4). What is the area of the circle? (Enter the coefficient of π only.)
questions.explanation: The radius equals the distance from the center (0,0) to the point (3,4). r = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Area = πr² = 25π. Coefficient = 25.
questions.trap: Adding the coordinates: r = 3 + 4 = 7, area = 49π. The radius requires the distance formula, not addition.

questions.question: Two circles of radii 3 and 4 are externally tangent to each other. A line is drawn tangent to both circles from the outside (an external common tangent). What is the length of the tangent segment between the two points of tangency?
questions.explanation: For two externally tangent circles the distance between centers is d = 3 + 4 = 7. The external common tangent segment has length √(d² − (r₁ − r₂)²) = √(49 − 1) = √48 = 4√3. (Equivalently 2√(r₁r₂) = 2√12 = 4√3.)
questions.trap: Using r₁ + r₂ in the formula for external tangent instead of r₁ − r₂, getting √(49−49) = 0.
questions.ets_note: Numeric options not ascending (2√3,4√3,2√7,4√7,2√33); distractors arbitrary.

questions.question: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle of radius 6. What is the length of a side of the triangle? (Enter your answer in the form a√b, where a and b are positive integers.)
questions.explanation: For an equilateral triangle with side s, the circumradius R = s/√3. So 6 = s/√3 → s = 6√3. Alternatively: R = s/(√3) comes from R = s√3/3 = s/√3. Verify: circumradius of equilateral triangle = s/√3 = (6√3)/√3 = 6. ✓
questions.trap: Using the formula R = s/2 (which applies to a square), getting s = 12.
questions.ets_note: Radical-entry format not possible in ETS numeric entry; textbook formula recall.

changes: "circle circumscribed around triangle" -> "triangle inscribed in a circle"
shortened format instruction (answer form 6√3 is fixed by the key)

questions.question: A circle of radius 10 has a chord that subtends a central angle of 90°. What is the area of the minor segment (the region bounded by the chord and the minor arc)?
questions.explanation: Minor segment = sector − triangle. The 90° sector = (90/360)π(10²) = 25π. The triangle formed by the two radii and the chord is right-angled at the center with legs 10 and 10, so its area = ½(10)(10) = 50. Segment = 25π − 50.
questions.trap: Computing the sector area without subtracting the triangle area, or using the full circle area minus the triangle.
questions.ets_note: Numeric options not ascending (25pi-100 is negative, listed second); one-step segment labelled hard.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Segment as 90° sector minus right triangle; two standard formulas chained.

questions.question:
A circle has radius r. A square is inscribed in the circle.

Quantity A: Area of the circle
Quantity B: 1.6 times the area of the square
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: A square inscribed in a circle of radius r has diagonal 2r, so its side is r√2 and its area is 2r². Quantity A = circle area = πr² ≈ 3.14r². Quantity B = 1.6 × 2r² = 3.2r². Since 3.14r² < 3.2r², Quantity B is greater.
questions.trap: Approximating π/2 ≈ 1.57 and comparing to 1.6: since π/2 < 1.6, the circle area is less than 1.6 times the square area. Students who think π > 3.2 get the wrong answer.

questions.question: Three circles, each with radius 2, are mutually externally tangent to each other. What is the area of the region bounded between the three circles (the 'gap' in the middle)?
questions.explanation: Joining the three centers gives an equilateral triangle of side 2 + 2 = 4, with area (√3/4)(4²) = 4√3. Inside it, each circle contributes a 60° sector of radius 2, totaling 3 × (60/360)π(2²) = 3 × (1/6)(4π) = 2π. The central gap = 4√3 − 2π.
questions.trap: Using r = 2 but computing sectors with r = 4 (the side length), or forgetting to multiply sector area by 3.
questions.ets_note: Fine geometry; 'gap in middle' phrasing informal, triangle method not hidden.

questions.question: A circle has equation x² + y² − 6x + 8y − 11 = 0. What is the radius of this circle?
questions.trap: Reading the equation as r² = 11 (using only the constant term) and reporting r = √11.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Complete the square to rewrite the equation in standard form, then read the radius; algebra plus circle equation.

questions.question: A goat is tied to the corner of a 10×8 rectangular barn with a rope of length 14. What is the total area the goat can graze? (Assume the barn blocks the goat's path.)
questions.explanation: At the corner the barn blocks a 90° wedge, so the goat grazes a 270° sector of radius 14: (3/4)π(14²) = 147π. Wrapping past the 8-ft side leaves 14 − 8 = 6 ft, adding (1/4)π(6²) = 9π. Wrapping past the 10-ft side leaves 14 − 10 = 4 ft, adding (1/4)π(4²) = 4π. Total = 147π + 9π + 4π = 160π.
questions.trap: Only computing the main 270° sector and ignoring the area accessible when the rope wraps around the barn corners.
questions.ets_note: Classic goat problem; plausible but cliched.

questions.question:
In circle O, chord AB has length 10. Chord CD passes through the center O (so CD is a diameter). AB and CD intersect at point P, where AP = 4.

Quantity A: CP × PD
Quantity B: 24
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords theorem: AP × PB = CP × PD. AP = 4, AB = 10, so PB = 10 − 4 = 6. Therefore CP × PD = AP × PB = 4 × 6 = 24. Quantity A = 24 = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Trying to find the actual values of CP and PD separately (which requires knowing the radius) rather than using the intersecting chords product directly.
questions.ets_note: Power-of-a-point in one step; hard label overstated; "so CD is a diameter" is redundant.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Intersecting chords theorem with PB=6; the diameter detail is a distractor.

questions.question: In circle O with radius 10, two chords AB and CD are parallel. The perpendicular distance between the chords is 14. If AB = 12, what is the length of CD?
questions.explanation: AB = 12, so half-chord = 6. Distance from center to AB: d₁ = √(10² − 6²) = √(100−36) = √64 = 8. Since the perpendicular distance between the chords is 14 and 2r = 20, the chords must be on opposite sides of the center (8 + d₂ = 14 → d₂ = 6, or they're both on same side: |8 − d₂| = 14 → d₂ = −6, impossible). So d₂ = 6. Half of CD = √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8. CD = 16.
questions.trap: Placing both chords on the same side of the center: d₂ = 14 − 8 = 6, which still gives CD = 16, so the answer is correct. But some students compute d₂ = 8 + 14 = 22 > 10 = radius, which is impossible, and get confused.
questions.ets_note: Trap and explanation muddled about same-side case; trap does not match an option.

questions.question: Circle O has radius 5. Point P is outside the circle, with OP = 13. A secant from P passes through the circle, entering at point A and exiting at point B (so P, A, B are collinear with A between P and B). PA = 3. Which of the following are true? Select all that apply.
options: B. The tangent from P to the circle has length 12
D. The power of point P = 75
questions.explanation: Power of P = OP² − r² = 169 − 25 = 144. From PA × PB = 144 with PA = 3, PB = 48, so AB = 48 − 3 = 45, and the tangent length = √144 = 12. Checking: (A) PB = 48 ≠ 25 ✗; (B) tangent = 12 ✓; (C) AB = 45 ≠ 22 ✗; (D) power = 144 ≠ 75 ✗; (E) OA and OB are radii = 5 ✓. So B and E.
questions.trap: Not applying power of a point correctly: using PA × PB = r² instead of OP² − r².
questions.ets_note: Given PA=3 contradicts OP=13, r=5 (min PA is 8); secant-tangent power theorem not ETS syllabus.

questions.question: A circle of radius r is rolled inside a circle of radius 4r without slipping. If the small circle starts with its center at distance 3r from the big circle's center, and completes one full trip around the interior of the big circle, how many complete rotations does the small circle make about its own center?
questions.explanation: When a circle of radius r rolls inside a circle of radius R, the small circle's center travels on a circle of radius R − r = 4r − r = 3r. The path length of the small circle's center = 2π(3r). Each full rotation of the small circle covers a distance of 2πr (its circumference). Number of rotations = 2π(3r) / (2πr) = 3. The small circle makes 3 complete rotations.
questions.trap: Using R = 4r as the path radius instead of R − r = 3r, and getting 2π(4r)/(2πr) = 4 rotations.
questions.ets_note: Rolling-circle rotation count is above GRE scope; stem muddled about start position.

questions.question:
In a circle of radius r, one chord is at distance a from the center and a different chord is at distance b from the center, where 0 ≤ a < b < r.

Quantity A: Length of the first chord
Quantity B: Length of the second chord
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The chord length formula is 2√(r² − d²) where d is the perpendicular distance from the center. Since a < b, we have a² < b², so r² − a² > r² − b², thus √(r² − a²) > √(r² − b²), and 2√(r² − a²) > 2√(r² − b²). A chord closer to the center is always longer. Quantity A > Quantity B.
questions.trap: Thinking a < b means the first chord is shorter (confusing distance from center with arc distance or position along the circle).
questions.ets_note: Chord lengths are handed over in the stem; one-step comparison labelled extreme_hard.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Chord-length formula is given; just note a smaller distance gives a larger value.

changes: removed the chord-length formulas from the stem

questions.question: Four unit circles (radius = 1) are arranged so that each circle is tangent to its two neighbors and all four are tangent to a large circle internally. What is the radius of the large circle? Enter as a decimal rounded to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The four unit circles have centers at (1,1), (−1,1), (−1,−1), (1,−1) — each at distance √2 from the origin. The large circle must be internally tangent to each small circle, so its radius R satisfies: distance from large center (origin) to small center = R − 1. Distance from origin to each small center = √(1²+1²) = √2. So R − 1 = √2 → R = 1 + √2 ≈ 1 + 1.4142 = 2.4142 ≈ 2.41.
questions.trap: Setting R = √2 (treating the large circle's radius as equal to the distance between centers rather than the distance plus the small radius).
questions.ets_note: Irrational answer forced into a rounded entry; label extreme_hard is overstated.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Place centers on a square at (±1,±1) and use tangency R-1=√2; needs a coordinate reframing but short.

questions.question: In a circle of radius 10, two chords intersect at a point P located 6 units from the center. One chord is divided by P into segments of lengths a and b; the other into segments c and d. What is the value of ab (which equals cd)?
questions.explanation: For any chord through an interior point P, the product of the two segments equals the power of P: r^2 - OP^2 = 10^2 - 6^2 = 100 - 36 = 64. The same value arises for every chord through P, so ab = cd = 64. (Check with the chord perpendicular to OP: each half is sqrt(100 - 36) = 8, and 8 x 8 = 64.)
questions.trap: Choice D reports r^2 and choice B reports OP^2, each dropping one term of the difference. Choice A, 16, is the length of the chord through P perpendicular to OP (2 x 8), a length mistaken for a product. Choice E, 128, adds the two equal products ab + cd instead of reporting the single common value.
questions.ets_note: Trap refers to nonexistent options (ab+cd=128, D). Option E odd for a determinable value; one-theorem question labelled extreme_hard.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Reframe by choosing the chord along the diameter through P (segments 4 and 16) or use power of a point; non-obvious but short.

changes: replaced banned 'E. It cannot be determined' with 128 (ab + cd)
replaced the unmotivated distractor 80 with 16, the length of the shortest chord through P
re-sorted ascending 16, 36, 64, 100, 128; answer letter is C
rewrote the trap field, which previously referenced statement-style options that do not exist in this item

questions.question:
A Reuleaux triangle is formed by three circular arcs, each centered at one vertex of an equilateral triangle with side s, and each arc connecting the other two vertices. Its 'width' (distance between any pair of parallel supporting lines) is exactly s.

Quantity A: Area of the Reuleaux triangle with width s
Quantity B: Area of a circle with diameter s
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Area of Reuleaux triangle = (1/2)(π − √3)s² ≈ (1/2)(3.1416 − 1.7321)s² ≈ (1/2)(1.4095)s² ≈ 0.7048s². Area of circle with diameter s (radius s/2): π(s/2)² = πs²/4 ≈ 0.7854s². Since 0.7048s² < 0.7854s², Quantity B > Quantity A.
questions.trap: Assuming the Reuleaux triangle, which has the same width as the circle, must have a larger area than the circle because it 'fills more space' — but the circle of the same width actually has greater area.
questions.ets_note: Obscure shape, needs sector-minus-triangle then decimal approximation; not ETS-like.

questions.question: A circle C₁ of radius 3 and a circle C₂ of radius 5 have their centers 10 units apart. A direct common external tangent touches C₁ at A and C₂ at B. What is the length of AB? Enter as an exact value (integer or simplified radical).
questions.explanation: For two circles with radii r₁ = 3, r₂ = 5, and center distance d = 10: Length of external common tangent = √(d² − (r₂ − r₁)²) = √(100 − (5−3)²) = √(100 − 4) = √96 = 4√6. Note: for EXTERNAL tangent, the formula uses (r₁ − r₂)² when the circles are on the same side, and (r₁ + r₂)² for internal tangent. Since both circles are external to each other (d = 10 > r₁ + r₂ = 8), external tangent length = √(d²−(r₁−r₂)²) = √(100−4) = √96 = 4√6.
questions.trap: Using the internal tangent formula √(d²−(r₁+r₂)²) = √(100−64) = 6, which gives the length of an internal (crossing) tangent, not the external tangent.
questions.ets_note: Formula lookup labelled extreme_hard; radical numeric entry unlike ETS; stem names 'direct common external tangent'.

questions.question:
Circle C₁ has radius r. Circle C₂ has a circumference equal to the area of C₁.

Quantity A: The radius of C₂
Quantity B: r²/2
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Area of C₁ = πr². This equals the circumference of C₂: 2πr₂ = πr² → r₂ = πr²/(2π) = r²/2. Quantity A = r₂ = r²/2 = Quantity B. The quantities are equal.
questions.trap: Students equate areas instead of setting area of C₁ = circumference of C₂. Setting πr² = πr₂² gives r₂ = r, so they compare r with r²/2, which depends on whether r > 2 or r < 2, and choose D.
questions.ets_note: Short derivation labelled extreme_hard.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Equate C2 circumference with C1 area and solve for r2; two formulas.

questions.question: An 8 × 8 square has four quarter-circles, each centered at a corner of the square with radius 4. What is the area of the square NOT covered by any of the four quarter-circles?
questions.explanation: Each quarter-circle has radius 4 and area = ¼π(4²) = 4π. Four quarter-circles total area = 4 × 4π = 16π. Since each quarter-circle sits in its own corner and the radius (4) equals exactly half the side length (8), adjacent quarter-circles meet at the midpoints of sides with zero overlap. Total covered area = 16π. Uncovered area = 64 − 16π.
questions.trap: Students compute one full circle (π × 4² = 16π) and subtract correctly — arriving at 64−16π by coincidence but for the wrong reason. A common error is computing only one quarter-circle's area (4π) and subtracting: 64−4π (choosing B).
questions.ets_note: Labelled extreme_hard but routine; trap text garbled ('coincidence'); no figure supplied.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Four corner quarter-circles sum to one circle of radius 4; subtract from square.

questions.question: In the xy-plane, one square has vertices (0, 0), (10, 0), (10, 10) and (0, 10), and a second square has vertices (5, 5), (11, 5), (11, 11) and (5, 11). What is the area of the region covered by at least one of the two squares?
questions.explanation: The first square has area 10 × 10 = 100 and the second has area 6 × 6 = 36. They overlap where 5 ≤ x ≤ 10 and 5 ≤ y ≤ 10, a 5-by-5 square of area 25. Adding the two areas counts that overlap twice, so the region covered by at least one square has area 100 + 36 − 25 = 111.
questions.trap: Students add the two areas and answer 136, forgetting that the overlap is counted twice. Students who subtract the whole smaller square answer 100; only the 5-by-5 corner of the smaller square lies inside the larger one.
questions.ets_note: Orientation unspecified and 'share exactly one vertex' contradicts the corner-at-center placement.

changes: replaced the four-sentence description of the placement, which left the smaller square's orientation unstated and said the squares 'share exactly one vertex' while also placing a corner of one at the center of the other, with the coordinates of all eight vertices
asked for 'the area of the region covered by at least one of the two squares' instead of 'the total area of the union', which is set vocabulary
the overlap, the arithmetic and the stored answer 111 are unchanged

A rectangle has integer dimensions and area 60. Select all values below that are possible perimeters of this rectangle.

A. 32
B. 34

questions.trap: Students include D=62 by assuming any even number between 32 and 122 is achievable, not verifying that l+w=31 with lw=60 requires non-integer dimensions.
questions.ets_note: Options duplicated inside stem text; modest work labelled extreme_hard.
